newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Nothing bends bonds out of shape.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Nothing bends bonds out of shape.

text.p: Neither U.S. May retail sales nor the turmoil within the European Monetary Union can bend the U.S. Treasury 30-year bond out of shape -- or force its yield out of its range, analysts predicted.

"We have been in a range for ages. Probably, we are at the lower end of that range in terms of bond yield, in the 6-3/4- to 7-1/8-percent area," said MCM MoneyWatch senior economist Astrid Adolfson. "Nothing will get us out of there."
The benchmark bond yield has fluctuated within that range since late February.

Bond yields have fluctuated in the 6.75-percent to 7.15-percent range since February 26 as the market alternatively gropped for signs an economic slowdown or hints of the next move by the Federal Reserve.

"We won't get out of this range because nothing has changed. The economy is strong and the Fed is still a threat," said Adolfson who stressed "with the unemployment rate at 4.8 percent, the economy is not falling back significantly."
Adolfson predicted the U.S. May retail sales, scheduled for release on Thursday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are "not going to be enough to change views about the Fed."
The consensus forecast in a Reuters poll puts retail sales up 0.4 percent in May following a 0.3-percent drop in April.
Adolfson did not rule out the possibility that an upward revision of the April retail sales number may somehwat pressure Treasuries, "though not be a problem."
Adolfson said U.S. Treasuries should continue to benefit -- but only to a certain extent -- from a move out of the European debt affected by uncertainty over the European Monetary Union (EMU).
"But I don't think this will go too far because there are a lot of non-EMU countries to invest in," she added.

Ed McKelvey, senior economist at Goldman, Sachs and Co., anticipated that the long bond yield would test the lower end of its range on soft May retail sales "because this should reinforce the perception the Fed is not going to do anything."
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is meeting on July 1-2. On March 25, the Fed raised the federal funds rate to 5.50 percent and kept it at that level on May 20.
However, like Adolfson, McKelvey did not expect the long bond yield to set in a new range.
"We are getting set up for the summer," predicted McKelvey who noted volatility already died down this week.
The other main report of the week, the Producer Price Index for May, scheduled for release on Friday, is not likely to provide much incentive for trading either, traders said.
In late trading on Wednesday, the 30-year bond was quoted at 97-12/32, up 4/32, to yield 6.83 percent.
Fed funds are seen opening slightly above their 5-1/2 percent target on Thursday.
The Fed added temporary reserves to the banking system on Wednesday via overnight system repurchase agreements. It also permanently added reserves with a $1.649-billion coupon pass.
